title: Friuli to Milan: the Wooden Theatre and the Idea of the World
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Friuli and Padua: Formation of a Rhetor

stops.name: Zoppola, the castle of his birth
stops.campa: A boy is born in Friuli, in the flat country between the Tagliamento and the Livenza, in a year the chroniclers will later disagree on: some say Portogruaro, some Udine, some this castle of Zoppola. His father's people come out of Delminium, an old Dalmatian town across the Adriatic, and the boy will take that town's name for his own: Camillo Delminio. Nothing marks the birth as extraordinary yet. But the region itself is a crossing-place, march of empires, and the boy who is born here will spend his life building a theatre meant to be the crossing-place of everything that has ever been said.
suggested_refs: The castle of Zoppola in Friuli, one of three sites the eighteenth-century memoirists give for his birth
sources: Gian-Giuseppe Liruti, Notizie delle vite ed opere scritte da' Letterati del Friuli, Tomo Terzo (Udine, 1780)
Judita Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre (CEU MA thesis, 2021), p. 10
Wikipedia, 'Giulio Camillo'

stops.name: Padua, the University, philosophy and jurisprudence
stops.campa: At Padua, seat of the most famous Aristotelian school in Italy, Camillo studies philosophy and jurisprudence among the sons of half of Europe's nobility. He is quick, ambitious, and already in love with rhetoric more than with law. Scholars will later wonder whether the young Camillo crossed paths here or later in Bologna with the astronomer Copernicus, who studies at Padua in these same years; no record proves it, but the two disciplines, the ordering of the heavens and the ordering of memory, will both obsess him for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo del Bo, seat of the University of Padua, where Camillo studied philosophy and law
sources: Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13
Kate Robinson, A Search for the Source of the Whirlpool of Artifice (PhD thesis, Glasgow, 2003), p. 2

stops.name: San Vito al Tagliamento, teacher of eloquence and logic
stops.campa: Back in his own country, Camillo takes a post teaching eloquence and logic at the academy of San Vito al Tagliamento, seat of the lords who will soon give their name, Liviana, to a grander academy at Pordenone. He is a schoolmaster among the market towns of Friuli, drilling boys in Cicero's periods and Aristotle's figures, but he already speaks of memory as something more than a trick for orators: a ladder, if rightly built, by which the mind might climb to see everything at once, the way God sees it.
suggested_refs: The old schools of San Vito al Tagliamento, seat of the Lords of San Vito
sources: Liruti, Notizie delle vite ed opere
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 10

stops.name: Pordenone, the Accademia Liviana
stops.campa: In 1508 Camillo joins the short-lived Accademia Liviana at Pordenone, gathered under the patronage of the Lords of San Vito, called Liviani. Here he sits among poets and physicians of real standing: Girolamo Fracastoro, who will one day name syphilis and write of contagion in verse; Giovanni Cotta and Andrea Navagero, Venetian humanists of the first rank. It is a small academy and it will not outlast a generation, but it teaches Camillo that a room of the right minds, arranged in the right order, is itself a kind of memory theatre before he has built one of wood.
suggested_refs: Records of the Accademia Liviana di Pordenone, 1508-1537
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giulio Camillo'
Centro Culturale Augusto Del Noce, 'Il Pordenone e la Signoria Liviana (1508-1537)'

segments.name: Venice: The Sestiere di San Polo

stops.name: Venice, lodging by the house of Aldus Manutius
stops.campa: Camillo takes lodging in the Sestiere di San Polo, hard by the house of Aldus Manutius, whose press has already put Aristotle and Aldus's italic Virgil into the hands of half of literate Europe. The printing quarter hums with proof-sheets and Greek type. To live here is to live at the address of the New Learning itself. Camillo, still a provincial schoolmaster by trade, begins to be known among the men who correct Aldus's texts and argue in his courtyard: the beginning of a Venetian fame that will, within twenty years, reach as far as the court of France.
suggested_refs: The Aldine dolphin-and-anchor device, mark of the press whose neighborhood Camillo made his own
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giulio Camillo'
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13

stops.name: Venice, the friendship of Erasmus of Rotterdam
stops.campa: Among the Venetians whom Camillo comes to know is a visiting Dutchman correcting proofs for Aldus: Desiderius Erasmus. The two men are on easy terms in these Venetian years, close enough that Erasmus will later still call him an old acquaintance. It is a friendship the years will test hard: twenty years on, when Camillo's wooden Theatre is the talk of two kingdoms, this same Erasmus will judge it a dangerous folly. But in Venice, in the printing-house years, Camillo is simply one more clever young Italian in a city full of them.
suggested_refs: Erasmus's Epistolae, naming Camillo among his Venetian acquaintance
sources: P. S. Allen, ed., Erasmi Epistolae, vols. IX-X
Frances A. Yates, The Art of Memory (1966), ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, the circle of Titian, Aretino, Bembo, and Serlio
stops.campa: Camillo's Venice widens: he comes to know the painter Titian, already the most sought brush in the lagoon; Pietro Bembo, arbiter of the Italian tongue; the sharp-penned Pietro Aretino, whom he will correspond with for the rest of his life; and Sebastiano Serlio, the architect, whose treatises on the ancient theatre Camillo will one day plunder for his own reversed design. He is not yet the famous Camillo. He is a bright provincial finding his level among men who will, within a generation, be called the great age of Venetian art and letters.
suggested_refs: Titian's Venetian portraits of the circle Camillo frequented
sources: Wikipedia, 'Giulio Camillo'
Lina Bolzoni, The Gallery of Memory (trans. Parzen, 2001)

stops.name: Rome, before Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo
stops.campa: Camillo travels to Rome and comes into the orbit of Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo, the great Augustinian prior whose Scechina is the master text of Christian Kabbalah in Italy, and whose circle includes the Venetian friar Francesco Giorgi. From this meeting, scholars will trace the current that runs into Camillo's Theatre: the Sephirot, the three worlds, the angels ranked over the planets, all drawn from the Kabbalah that Pico della Mirandola had baptized into Christian philosophy a generation before. Camillo leaves Rome carrying, half-formed, the scaffolding on which his whole Theatre will one day be raised.
suggested_refs: Egidio da Viterbo's Scechina, key text of the Christian Kabbalah Camillo drew on
sources: François Secret, I Cabbalisti Cristiani del Rinascimento (2001), p. 278
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, pp. 4-5, citing Yates and Bolzoni

stops.name: Venice, the first stirring of the Theatre
stops.campa: Back in Venice, Camillo begins in earnest the labor that will occupy him for the next twenty-five years: the Idea of the Theatre. Johann Sturm will later call it the fruit of forty years' work, counting back from Camillo's death almost exactly to this year. He does not yet call it a building. He calls it, in the treatise he is drafting, a workshop where every human thought might be given its own fixed place, to be found again at will, the whole of learning laid out at a glance the way a merchant lays out his goods on a table.
stops.quote: The reason is from knowing that in the great workshop of 'Teatro' are disposed through loci and images all the places necessary to locate and minister to all human concepts, everything in the entire world, not only those pertaining to all sciences and the noble and mechanic arts.
stops.quote_source: Trattato dell'Imitatione (Treatise on Imitation), trans. Kate Robinson
suggested_refs: Johann Sturm's note (Linguae Latinae resolvendae ratio, 1581) calling the Idea the fruit of a forty-year effort
sources: Johann Sturm, Linguae Latinae resolvendae ratio (Strasbourg, 1581)
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 10
socks-studio.com, 'Spatializing Knowledge: Giulio Camillo's Theatre of Memory (1519-1544)'

stops.name: Bologna, the chair of Dialectics
stops.campa: Camillo is given, for some years, a chair of Dialectics at the University of Bologna, oldest of the schools of Europe. He lectures on logic to law students and future physicians, and he is remembered, even by his rivals, as a teacher who could turn dry syllogism into something like poetry. It is here, Torquato Tasso will later say, that Camillo shows for the first time since Dante that rhetoric itself is a kind of poetry: not ornament laid over thought, but thought's own natural shape.
suggested_refs: The University of Bologna, where Camillo held the chair of Dialectics
sources: Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI, citing Tasso's remark

stops.name: Bologna, the fame of the great inventor
stops.campa: Word of Camillo's method spreads beyond the lecture hall. Ariosto, finishing his Orlando Furioso, will place him among the noblemen of the final canto as one who leads readers 'by a shorter pathway to the Ascraean font divine,' the fountain of Hesiod himself. Liruti, writing two centuries later, will simply call him 'Giulio Camillo, great inventor of ways to make the sciences easy.' None of this fame yet has a building attached to it. It is the fame of a man everyone agrees is extraordinary and no one has quite seen prove it.
suggested_refs: Ludovico Ariosto, Orlando Furioso, canto 46, naming Camillo among the illustrious
sources: Ludovico Ariosto, Orlando Furioso 46.12
Liruti, Notizie delle vite ed opere, p. 70

stops.name: Venice, the reversal: the spectator upon the stage
stops.campa: The design comes clear to Camillo: he will not build a memory-room for a single orator to walk through, as the ancients taught, but a theatre proper, on the model Vitruvius gives for Rome, with its seven gangways and rising seats. Then he inverts it entire. In his Theatre no audience sits watching a play; a single spectator stands where the stage would be, and looks outward and upward at the whole cosmos, ranked in the seats before him, legible at a glance from that one point. Scholar and orator alike is to become spectator of everything at once.
stops.quote: Now if the ancient orators, wishing to place from day to day the parts of the speeches which they had to recite, confided them to frail places as frail things, it is right that we, wishing to store up eternally the eternal nature of all things which can be expressed in speech, should assign them to eternal places. Our high labour, therefore, has been to find an order in these seven measures, capacious and distinct from one another, and which will keep the mind awake and move the memory.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro (Florence, 1550), trans. Frances Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: Vitruvius, De architectura, Book V, chapter 6, on the seven gangways of the Roman theatre, which Camillo inverts
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, pp. 1-3

stops.name: Venice, first grade: the seven pillars and the planets
stops.campa: On the lowest and most honored grade of the Theatre, Camillo places not the seven Sephirot themselves, too remote from ordinary understanding, but the seven planets that stand in for them: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, each ranked with its Sephirah and its governing angel. Ancient theatres seated the great in the lowest rows; Camillo does the same with meaning, since from these fundamental measures, once truly known, the mind can climb into the supercelestial world of the Ideas or descend into the elemental world spread out above.
stops.quote: Solomon in the ninth chapter of Proverbs says that wisdom has built herself a house and has founded it on seven pillars. By these columns, signifying most stable eternity, we are to understand the seven Sephiroth of the supercelestial world, which are the seven measures of the fabric of the celestial and inferior worlds.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 9, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: The seven Sephirot of Christian Kabbalah, ranked with the seven planets on the Theatre's lowest gate
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Lu Beery Wenneker, An Examination of L'idea del theatro (PhD diss., Pittsburgh, 1970)

stops.name: Venice, the Banquet, second grade
stops.campa: Above the planets, Camillo sets the image of a Banquet on every gate of the second grade: Homer's tale that Ocean once feasted all the gods together. Ocean, Camillo explains, is the waters of wisdom that existed before all created matter, and the feasting gods are the divine Ideas gathering to bring forth the world. It is his image for the first day of creation, the elements still simple and unmixed, and he means the reader, gazing at banquet after banquet across seven gates, to feel Genesis itself, In the beginning, opening beneath the picture.
stops.quote: The second grade of the Theatre will have depicted on all its gates the same image, and this will be a banquet. Homer feigns that Ocean made a banquet for all the gods, nor was it without lofty mysterious meanings that this lofty poet invented this fiction.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 17, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: Homer's tale of Ocean's banquet for the gods (Iliad I.423-5), image of the Theatre's second grade
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Macrobius, Commentary on the Dream of Scipio, on the gods who feast with Jupiter as the planets

stops.name: Venice, the Cave of the Nymphs, third grade
stops.campa: The third grade rises with a Cave on every gate: not Plato's cave of shadows, Camillo is careful to say, but the Cave of the Nymphs from Homer's Odyssey, where nymphs weave at looms of stone and bees pass ceaselessly in and out. Following Porphyry's ancient reading of that cave, Camillo makes the weaving nymphs and laboring bees stand for the mixing of the four simple elements into all the compounded things of the world, each cave keeping, planet by planet, the particular mixture proper to its nature.
stops.quote: The third grade will have depicted on each of its gates a Cave, which we call the Homeric Cave to differentiate it from that which Plato describes in his Republic.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 29, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: Porphyry, De antro nympharum, the ancient commentary on Homer's Cave that Camillo draws on
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Homer, Odyssey XIII.102ff.

stops.name: Venice, the Gorgon Sisters, fourth grade
stops.campa: The fourth grade belongs to the interior man, mind and soul, the noblest of God's creatures made in his own image. Its image, strange to a first glance, is Hesiod's three Gorgon Sisters, who share only a single eye between them. Camillo takes this from Kabbalist teaching on the three souls of man, vegetable, sensitive, and rational, seeing through one another as the sisters see through their one eye. Behind each gate wait the volumes proper to the interior man, ranked planet by planet, so that the whole science of the soul stands open at this level of the climb.
stops.quote: Let us now rise to the fourth grade belonging to the interior man, the most noble of God's creatures, which He made in his own image and similitude.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 53, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: Hesiod's Gorgon Sisters, sharing one eye, the Theatre's image for the three souls of man
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Hesiod, Shield of Hercules, l. 230

stops.name: Venice, Pasiphae and the Bull, fifth grade
stops.campa: On the fifth grade the soul is joined at last to the body, and the leading image is Pasiphae enamoured of the Bull: for the Platonists teach that the descending soul, changing its fiery vehicle for an airy one as it falls through the spheres, comes at last to desire gross matter itself, exactly as the queen of Crete desired the beast. Beneath this image on every gate wait the sciences of the exterior man, his body's parts and humors, each assigned, at the foot of the gate, to its ruling sign of the zodiac.
stops.quote: For she, being enamoured of the Bull, signifies the soul which, according to the Platonists, falls into a state of desiring the body.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, p. 67, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: The zodiac Bulls at the foot of the fifth grade's gates, marking the parts of the human body
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, the Sandals of Mercury, sixth grade
stops.campa: The sixth grade is crowned on every gate with the winged Sandals of Mercury, which the poets say the messenger god puts on when he goes to execute the will of the gods. Under this image Camillo files everything a man can do by nature alone, without the aid of any learned art: the plain activities of ordinary human life, walking, working, trading, ruling a household. It is the grade just below the arts proper, the last rung before invention, the ordinary motion of the world before Prometheus brings down his fire.
stops.quote: The sixth grade of the Theatre has on each of the gates of the planets the Sandals, and other ornaments, which Mercury puts on when he goes to execute the will of the gods, as the poets feign. Thereby the memory will be awakened to find beneath them all the operations which man can perform naturally, and without any art.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: The winged sandals of Mercury, emblem of the Theatre's sixth grade
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Venice, Prometheus, seventh grade
stops.campa: At the summit, the seventh and highest grade, Camillo sets Prometheus with his stolen, lighted torch above every gate: the Titan who taught men the arts and sciences of the gods. Under this image he files all the noble arts and the vile ones alike, and religion, and law, the full harvest of human invention built on everything the lower six grades have laid down. The design is complete in idea, though not one board of it is yet cut: from the simple elements of the Banquet to the fire of Prometheus, the entire chain of being, ranked and locatable at a glance.
stops.quote: The seventh grade is assigned to all the arts, both noble and vile, and above each gate is Prometheus with a lighted torch.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro, trans. Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
suggested_refs: Prometheus with his torch, crowning image of the Theatre's seventh and highest grade
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, ch. 3

segments.name: The Wooden Theatre for a King

stops.name: Venice, departure for France with Rangone and Muzio
stops.campa: Word of the design, and perhaps of a beginning of the carpentry, reaches the French ambassador in Venice, Lazare de Baïf, who carries report of it to his king. In 1530 Camillo sets out for France in the company of Count Claudio Rangone and his loyal friend Girolamo Muzio, a courtier who will stand at Camillo's side, on and off, for the rest of his life and will be the one, fourteen years hence, to take down his dying words. Camillo leaves Italy still a schoolmaster of local fame; he means to return the confidant of a king.
suggested_refs: Girolamo Muzio's Lettere, recording the journey to France with Count Claudio Rangone
sources: Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13
Girolamo Muzio, Lettere (Florence, 1590)
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Fontainebleau, before Francis I
stops.campa: Camillo is brought before Francis I, patron already of Leonardo's old age and soon to be the builder of a whole gallery of allegory at Fontainebleau. He lays out the Idea of a theatre that will hold, ranked and legible, the sum of everything Cicero and the ancients ever knew, and hints at deeper secrets besides, Kabbalist and Hermetic, to be given to no other man alive but the king. Francis is captivated. He gives Camillo money toward the work, with the promise of more, on the single condition that Camillo publish nothing of it without his royal leave.
suggested_refs: Francis I's five hundred ducats, first payment toward the Theatre's completion
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13

stops.name: Venice, the return to perfect the work
stops.campa: Camillo returns to Italy to bring the wooden Theatre nearer completion before showing it again at the French court, and in Venice he sets down, in a manuscript discourse on his own project, the philosophical ground beneath the carpentry: a borrowed idea from Avicenna, that the human soul carries within it a hidden power to act upon the outer world, to bend things to its will, wherever the soul's affection for a thing is great enough. It is the same claim, restated in the language of the philosophers, that the Theatre itself will make silently through its images: that to see rightly is already to hold power.
stops.quote: Avicenna's conclusions in the sixth book on nature are very appealing to me, where he says that there is a certain capacity in our soul to change things and to make them obey us, while our soul is attracted by a great affection for them.
stops.quote_source: Discorso in materia del suo theatro (1532), trans. in Bolzoni, The Gallery of Memory
suggested_refs: Camillo's Discorso in materia del suo theatro, first sketch of the Theatre's rationale
sources: Bolzoni, The Gallery of Memory, p. 139
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Padua, Viglius Zuichemus hears the rumor
stops.campa: In Padua the young Frisian jurist Viglius Zuichemus, a correspondent and admirer of Erasmus, hears everyone talking of a certain Giulio Camillo who has built, they say, a wonderful amphitheatre: whoever is admitted to it as spectator will be able to discourse on any subject as fluently as Cicero himself. Viglius takes it at first for a traveler's fable, until Battista Egnazio, a scholar he trusts, confirms that the thing is real: an architect who has drawn up, in certain fixed places, everything that can be found in Cicero, arranged by orders and grades with stupendous labor and, Viglius begins to suspect, something more than merely human skill.
suggested_refs: Erasmus, Epistolae, ed. Allen, IX, p. 479, preserving Viglius's first report of the rumor
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI, quoting Erasmus, Epistolae IX, p. 479

stops.name: Venice, Viglius inspects the wooden Theatre
stops.campa: Viglius travels to Venice and Camillo himself admits him: an object big enough for two men to stand inside together, of wood, marked with many images, and full of little boxes, various orders and grades rising around them. Camillo shows him mass upon mass of paper, sentences of Cicero broken down and refiled by subject until Viglius, who thought he knew how rich an author Cicero was, is astonished at how much more can be drawn out of him. Camillo stammers over Latin, his pen having half-ruined his spoken tongue, but grows fluent and strange the moment he begins to explain, as though stupefied himself, what the Theatre means and does.
stops.quote: A built or constructed mind and soul... a windowed one. All things that the human mind can conceive, and which we cannot see with the corporeal eye, after being collected together by diligent meditation, may be expressed by certain corporeal signs in such a way that the beholder may at once perceive with his eyes everything that is otherwise hidden in the depths of the human mind.
stops.quote_source: Camillo's own description of the Theatre, recorded in Viglius Zuichemus's letter to Erasmus, 8 June 1532 (Erasmus, Epistolae, ed. Allen, X, pp. 29-30)
suggested_refs: Viglius Zuichemus's letter of 8 June 1532, the single eyewitness account of the Theatre standing and entered
sources: Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI, quoting Erasmus, Epistolae X, pp. 29-30
Douglas Radcliff-Umstead, 'Giulio Camillo's Emblems of Memory', Yale French Studies 47 (1972), p. 47

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, Erasmus answers, the tragedy in study
stops.campa: Erasmus, settled now at Freiburg, receives Viglius's astonished account and is not persuaded. He has spent his life arguing that memory is a plain and rational faculty, trained by ordinary method, and he has no patience for machines that promise Ciceronian eloquence by magic and Kabbalah besides. In his reply he judges that a thing capable of stirring up such excitement in the schools of Italy could produce as great a tragedy in study as Luther's had produced in religion: an old friend's fame turned, in a single letter, into a warning.
suggested_refs: Erasmus's letter of 5 July 1532, comparing the Theatre's stir to Luther's in religion
sources: Erasmus, Epistolae, ed. Allen, X
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 11

stops.name: Paris, the amphitheatre built for the king
stops.campa: By 1534 Camillo is settled at the French court, and the physician Jacques Bording writes to Étienne Dolet that Camillo has lately arrived to instruct the king and is constructing here an amphitheatre for the king, for the purpose of marking out divisions of memory. Whatever wood and glue and carved image the Venetian model amounted to, a version of it now stands, or is standing, somewhere near the French court, drawing courtiers and scholars to see the wonder that all Italy has talked of for two years.
suggested_refs: Jacques Bording's letter to Étienne Dolet, describing the amphitheatre under construction for Francis I
sources: R. C. Christie, Etienne Dolet (London, 1880), p. 142
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Paris, the lion that would not harm him
stops.campa: A story runs through the court that Camillo himself is glad to repeat. He goes one day with the Cardinal of Lorraine, the poet Luigi Alamanni, and other gentlemen to see the king's wild beasts, and a lion breaks loose and comes straight toward the party. The gentlemen scatter; Camillo, heavy-bodied and slow, alone stands his ground, less from courage, the tale-tellers admit, than from simple inability to run. The lion circles him, nuzzles him, and is driven off unharmed. All present agree it is because he stands, as his Theatre teaches, under the sign and virtue of the Sun.
suggested_refs: Giuseppe Betussi, Il Raverta (Venice, 1544), the earliest telling of the lion story
sources: Betussi, Il Raverta, ed. Zonta (Bari, 1912), p. 133
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Paris, illness and the letters to Aretino
stops.campa: The years at the French court grow harder. Camillo writes often to Pietro Aretino in Venice, confessing that he is frequently ill and that the great work drags, never finished, never quite fit to be shown whole. Francis I, who once promised so much, lets the ducats come more slowly; by hint of a later letter of Erasmus to Viglius, the flow of French gold has never matched Camillo's hopes. Sometime around this year Camillo lets go of the French court for good, the Theatre still incomplete, the king's secret still ungiven, and turns back toward Italy.
suggested_refs: Camillo's correspondence with Pietro Aretino, recording his illness and the unfinished work
sources: Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI, citing Erasmus, Epist. X, p. 226

segments.name: Milan: The Marchese and the Bed of Wisdom

stops.name: Venice, back in Italy, out of a patron
stops.campa: According to Girolamo Muzio's own account, the great man is back in Italy by 1543, his hopes at the French court exhausted, his Theatre still standing unfinished in the world's memory rather than in any one room. He is, for the first time in thirteen years, without a patron sure enough to carry the work to its end. He is over sixty, heavy, often unwell. Whatever is left of the forty-year labor Sturm will later speak of must now be gathered and given to someone, quickly, or lost with him.
suggested_refs: Girolamo Muzio's Lettere, recording Camillo's return to Italy in 1543
sources: Muzio, Lettere, p. 66ff.
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Milan, Muzio's mediation and the Marchese's offer
stops.campa: Muzio brings word of his old friend to Alfonso d'Avalos, the Marchese del Vasto, Spanish governor of Milan and commander of Charles V's armies in Italy, already patron to Ariosto and Aretino and sitter more than once for Titian's brush. The Marchese asks whether anything has come of Camillo's long hopes at the French court; hearing that it has not, he offers a pension in exchange for being taught the Theatre's secret himself. Warned by Muzio that many scholars doubt Camillo's whole enterprise, the Marchese answers simply that genuine or not, he wants it.
suggested_refs: Titian's portraits of Alfonso d'Avalos, Marchese del Vasto, Camillo's last patron
sources: Muzio, Lettere, p. 67ff.
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 13

stops.name: Milan, the meeting with the Marchese del Vasto
stops.campa: The meeting takes place in Milan before the year turns, and it is enough to seal the arrangement: Camillo will spend what remains of his life as del Vasto's pensioner, discoursing before him and in the academies of the city. It is, the record shows, the second offer of its kind Camillo has weighed; some say the Marchese had already sounded him out as early as 1539. Now, past sixty and out of the French king's favor, Camillo accepts. The secret he swore to Francis I he has already, quietly, begun to set free.
suggested_refs: Alfonso d'Avalos, Marchese del Vasto, Spanish governor of Milan and Camillo's final patron
sources: Wenneker, An Examination of L'idea del theatro, pp. 20-23
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 14

stops.name: Milan, seven mornings in adjoining beds
stops.campa: For seven mornings, from before dawn deep into the day, Camillo dictates the outline of forty years' labor to Girolamo Muzio, the two men reclining on adjoining beds in the same room, Camillo speaking, Muzio writing down every word. Scholars will later suspect the arrangement is deliberate on Camillo's part: a memory of Solomon's own lectulum, the bed of wisdom, from which the king of Israel is said to have spoken his proverbs. What comes out of these seven mornings is the manuscript that will become, after Camillo's death, the only complete account the world will ever have of the Theatre's Idea.
suggested_refs: The dictated manuscript of L'Idea del Theatro, taken down by Muzio over seven mornings
sources: Wenneker, An Examination of L'idea del theatro, pp. 23-27
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Milan, the death of Giulio Camillo
stops.campa: Soon after the seven mornings of dictation are finished, on the fifteenth of May 1544, Giulio Camillo dies in Milan. He is somewhere near sixty-four years old, by the uncertain count of his birth. The Theatre itself, the wooden object Viglius entered and touched twelve years before, has by now vanished from any record; when the French antiquary Montfaucon goes looking for it in the following century, he can find no trace. What survives is Muzio's manuscript, and the memory, already turning into legend, of the man everyone had called divine.
suggested_refs: The date of Camillo's death, 15 May 1544, recorded by Muzio and the early biographers
sources: Muzio, Lettere, p. 73
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 14
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Milan, burial in Santa Maria delle Grazie
stops.campa: Camillo is buried in the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie, the great Dominican church where, on the refectory wall a few steps from his grave, Leonardo's Last Supper has already been fading for forty years. The city that gave him his last patron gives him his last resting place. Within a decade admirers will be calling him a second Pico della Mirandola, a genius who died before delivering the whole fruit of a more than human intellect; within two centuries scholars will still be arguing whether the Theatre he left behind was wisdom or a beautiful, elaborate kind of confidence trick.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Camillo's burial place, steps from Leonardo's Last Supper
sources: Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 14
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI

stops.name: Florence, L'Idea del Theatro is published
stops.campa: Six years after Camillo's death, in April 1550, the printer Lorenzo Torrentino brings out at Florence, edited by Lodovico Domenichi, the little book that is all the world will ever have of the great design: L'Idea del Theatro dell'eccellentissimo M. Giulio Camillo. Domenichi's preface admits plainly that the entire machine of so superb an edifice can no longer be found. What is printed is the outline dictated in Milan, seven mornings, two men on adjoining beds: forty years of labor folded into a pamphlet the Theatre itself would have filed away on a single gate.
suggested_refs: L'Idea del Theatro dell'eccellen. M. Giulio Camillo (Florence: Lorenzo Torrentino, 1550), the editio princeps
sources: Wenneker, An Examination of L'idea del theatro, p. 185
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Internet Archive, L'idea del theatro dell'eccellen. M. Giulio Camillo

stops.name: Venice, the Jubilee reprint
stops.campa: Within months, the Venetian printer Baldassar Costantini rushes out his own edition, marked on the title page as the work of the Jubilee year, l'anno del Giubileo. Seven times seven years make a Jubilee in the old law of Leviticus, and the coincidence is fitting: Camillo's Theatre was itself built seven grades by seven planets, forty-nine gates. The book that could not save the man now travels where the wooden Theatre never did: Bruno will borrow its images for his own art of shadows within a generation; Kircher's engraved theatres of knowledge and the memory palaces the Jesuits carry to Ricci's China both walk, distantly, in the room Camillo built and never finished.
suggested_refs: Baldassar Costantini's Venice reprint of 1550, marked for the Jubilee year
sources: Wenneker, An Examination of L'idea del theatro, p. 185
Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
Uremović, Backstage at Camillo's Esoteric Theatre, p. 11
